newsitem.title: UK: ICCO agrees to overhaul cocoa stocks estimates.
newsitem.headline: ICCO agrees to overhaul cocoa stocks estimates.

text.p: Clelia Oziel
The International Cocoa Organization (ICCO), on advice from traders and analysts, has decided to overhaul the way it calculates world stocks with a view to improve accuracy.

A working group on stocks consisting of delegates, analysts and senior members of the trade concluded on Thursday that the ICCO's estimate of 1.4 million tonnes for end-September 1996 should be revised down.
"Most of us think 1.4 million is too high," said Robert Fish, the head of UK-based reseach group PCR Ltd who chaired the afternoon meeting.
Controversy stemmed from from a wide gap between the estimates of the ICCO and the UK-based trade and research group E.D.& F Man which pegged the 1995/96 stocks at 1.09 million.
PCR Ltd also put it lower at 1.2 million tonnes.
Obtaining accurate stock figures is crucial for the ICCO to implement a production management plan which envisages worldwide cuts based on a ratio of stocks to consumption of 34 percent.
Producers have been asked to curb output by 90,000 tonnes in the next three years to bring the ratio down from about 50 percent now as a result of record West African harvests.
But many warehouses are resistant to release what they regard as commercially sensitive information on stocks. The ICCO has a deadline of September 1997 to publish revised figures.

PCR's Fish said the main discrepancy between ICCO and trade figures could be 94,000 tonnes of unidentified cocoa which the ICCO used to bridge the data it receives from contributors and theoretical calculations based on consumption and grindings.

Total identified stocks were put at 1.310 million tonnes but the working group suggested that even here there was room for reduction. One possible item for revision was the ICCO's assumption of cocoa beans in transit totaling 90,000 tonnes.
"It can't be so high. Everything had been delivered by the end of September. The whole (futures market) structure had collapsed," said Fish, referring to a squeeze in futures prices.
The estimates for ports and manufacturers' working stocks could have had an element of double counting, Fish added.

Another suspect item was licensed U.S. warehouse stocks, which the ICCO put at 250,000 tonnes. Members of the group suggested that a high proportion of U.S. cocoa was Ecuadorian which weigh heavier than the ICCO's unit size of 60-kg.

A revision was also needed in ICCO's assumption that manufacturers' working stocks total two weeks of annual grindings in western Europe and five weeks in Americas. Just-in-time practices enable lower stocks.
Direct shipments in the Netherlands, however, would mean stocks there could be higher than two weeks.
Analysis of historical stocks going back 20 years revealed major discrepancies in producing countries like Ivory Coast and Ghana where an unusually large build-up of stocks was cited.
Steps were taken to eliminate these and Ghana agreed to send revised estimates of grindings.
The ICCO will also send a questionaire to warehouse keepers to gather stocks in September 1994 which it will compare with its own estimates.
